parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 5. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a city farm to ask about a visit for a group of children. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6. Dan: Good morning, Hollins City Farm, Dan speaking. Karen: Oh, hello. My name's Karen Webb, and I run a Cub Scout group in Eastfield. We're thinking of bringing the children to the farm for a day, and I wondered if you could tell me a bit about it. Dan: Of course. I'm the education officer here, so you've come to the right person. Karen: Great. I've never actually been, so how big is the farm? Dan: It's bigger than people expect for a farm in the middle of a city. We've got twelve acres altogether, which is about five hectares. Karen: Oh, that's quite big. And what animals do you have? Dan: We've got pigs, goats, chickens and rabbits, of course. We used to keep a couple of ponies, but they've moved to a farm in the countryside now. And our newest arrivals are three alpacas, which the children absolutely love. Karen: Alpacas! They'll be excited about that. What sort of activities can the children do? Dan: Well, most groups start with animal care. We don't do sheep shearing, I'm afraid, but the children can learn how to milk a goat, and they help to feed the animals too. Karen: That sounds fun. Do they do anything in the garden? Dan: Yes, we have a big vegetable garden. What they plant depends on the season. In the autumn it's usually garlic, but if you're coming in May, they'll be planting beans. Karen: We're thinking of the twentieth of May, so that works. Dan: Then there's a cooking session. We use eggs from our own hens, and the children make pancakes. We used to make omelettes, but that meant a lot of time standing at the cooker, so pancakes are much easier. Karen: I'm sure they'll enjoy eating them, too. Dan: They always do. And the last activity of the day is usually a craft session, using wool from a local sheep farm. The children make bracelets, which they can take home with them. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Karen: I'll need to explain to the parents why this kind of trip is worthwhile. What would you say the main benefits are? Dan: Well, for a start, looking after animals gives children a sense of responsibility. They have to think about another creature's needs, not just their own. Karen: Yes, that's a good point. Dan: And a lot of city children are quite nervous around animals at first. By the end of the day, most of them have learned to stay calm when they're near the animals, which is lovely to see. Karen: And what about the cost? Dan: For groups of up to twenty children, it's seven fifty per child. But if there are more than twenty, it goes down to six fifty. Karen: There'll be twenty-four of us, so that's good news. Dan: Adult helpers come free, and we recommend one adult for every six children. Karen: OK. And how do I make a booking? Dan: The best thing is to email me directly. My name's Dan Mercer. That's M, E, R, C, E, R. Karen: Thanks. I'll talk to the other leaders and get back to you. Dan: Great. Oh, and make sure everyone wears boots. It gets very muddy here. Karen: Will do. Thanks, Dan. Goodbye. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the chair of a community choir talking to members about recent events and future plans. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Chair: Good evening, everyone, and thank you all for coming to our end-of-season meeting. It's been a busy few months for the Riverside Community Choir, so I've got quite a lot to tell you. Chair: First, our trip to Bergen in Norway. Thirty-two of us went, and I think everyone agreed it was a wonderful weekend. Our concert in the city went very well, although the audience was smaller than we'd hoped. The sightseeing tour of the old harbour had to be cancelled because of the rain, which was a pity. But what most of you told me you enjoyed was the Saturday evening we spent with our host choir. We sang for each other, then all together, and it went on until nearly midnight. People are still talking about it. Chair: Now, as you know, next year the choir will be twenty years old. We talked about asking a composer to write a new piece for us, but the fees were simply too high. Our friends in Bergen are holding a festival for their anniversary, but that isn't really practical for a group of our size. So what we've decided to do is make a professional recording of some of our favourite pieces, and we'll sell the CD at our concerts. Chair: Fundraising has gone really well this year. The quiz night was fun, but it only raised about three hundred pounds. The cake sale in March made just over eight hundred, which was brilliant. But the sponsored walk beat everything, with nearly twelve hundred pounds. Thank you to everyone who took part. Chair: Next month, we'll be welcoming the Bergen choir here, and many of you have kindly offered to host singers. Their coach arrives at the community centre at six on Friday, so there's no need to go to the airport. On Saturday morning, there's a rehearsal at ten, but please don't feel you have to arrive early. After the rehearsal, we're taking everyone on a walking tour of the old town. The cafe in the market square is providing lunch, so there's no need to make sandwiches. The forecast isn't good, though, so please make sure your guests have waterproof clothing with them. Chair: On Sunday afternoon, we'll give our joint concert. Unfortunately, the children's choir from Saint Mark's School can't join us after all, as several of the children will be away. But I'm pleased to say that the local radio station will be recording the concert, and they'll broadcast part of it the following week. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Chair: The concert will be in Bramley Hall, in Bramley Park, and I've given you all a map, because some of our guests will want to explore the park before the concert starts. Chair: As you come in through the main gate, you'll see a small building immediately on your left, right beside the gate. That's the ticket office, and that's where the Bergen singers should collect their passes. Chair: Some of our guests use wheelchairs, and there are steps at the front of the hall, so they'll need the accessible entrance. That's at the back of the hall, on the side furthest from the main gate. Just follow the path round. Chair: If any of your guests have children with them, there's a good playground. Walk along the cross path to the right, all the way to the end, then turn left and go north, with the lake on your left. At the top, the path bends to the left, and the playground is just there, beyond the northern end of the lake. Chair: We're planning a picnic before the concert, weather permitting. We'll meet on the lawn between the hall and the lake, on the east side of the hall. Chair: And for anyone who fancies a walk, there's an old tower in the park with wonderful views. Take the cross path to the left, all the way to the end, and then turn right. That path goes north along the edge of the woods, and the tower is at the very end, in the corner of the park. Chair: Right, if there are no questions, let's move on to the music for next season. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two fashion design students, Hannah and Leo, discussing their final-year projects. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Hannah: Hi, Leo. I haven't seen you in the studio for ages. Leo: No, I've been working at home mostly. The final project has taken over my life. Hannah: You're making bags out of old jeans, aren't you? Leo: That's right. I collect jeans that people have thrown out, cut them up and turn them into bags. The actual sewing was fairly straightforward. I've been using the embroidery machine to decorate them, but I learned how to use that in the first year, so that wasn't new. Hannah: So what's been the best part? Leo: Honestly, the thing I'm proudest of is taking something that was going to end up in landfill and turning it into something people actually want to use. That's really satisfying. And I've loved trying out different ways of decorating the bags, like painting, patchwork and embroidery. Every bag's different. I've made about thirty so far, and I'm hoping to have fifty for the final exhibition. Hannah: Have you entered it for the college prize? Leo: Yes, but they won't announce the winners until June, so I'm not getting my hopes up. And I've been working completely on my own, which has been a bit lonely, to be honest. Hannah: Well, I think the bags sound great. My project's quite different. I've been looking at fabrics that change colour depending on temperature. Leo: Oh, using special dyes? Hannah: Yes. They've been around for decades, but people mainly thought of them as a novelty, like T-shirts that changed colour when you touched them. Some designers have used them in catwalk shows too, but that's really just for effect. Leo: I remember those T-shirts. So what could they be used for now? Hannah: Well, one idea is sportswear, so that coaches could see which muscles are working hardest. Leo: I'm not convinced by that. Athletes already have heart monitors and all sorts of sensors that give much more accurate information. Hannah: Maybe you're right. But I think they'd be really useful in clothes for babies. If a baby was getting a fever, the fabric would change colour, and parents would notice straight away. Leo: Yes, that's a great idea. Parents would definitely buy that. And what about hospitals? Bandages that change colour to show when a wound is getting infected? Hannah: That's already being researched, actually. And I agree, I think that's where the real future is. Leo: It's certainly more useful than handbags that change colour in the sun. Hannah: Ha, yes. Someone tried that a few years ago, and nobody bought them. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Leo: I've been reading a report on trends in the fashion industry for my dissertation. My tutor wants us to connect our own projects to what is happening in the wider industry, so it has been really useful. Hannah: Oh, that sounds interesting. What did it say? Leo: Well, one trend is the growth in apps for buying and selling second-hand clothes. Hannah: That's hardly new, is it? My sister and her friends have been using those apps for years. Leo: True. Then there's the question of what brands do with clothes they can't sell. Some of them just burn them or shred them. Hannah: That's terrible. France has banned it, hasn't it? I think our government should bring in a law like that, too. Leo: I agree. Another trend is clothing made from recycled plastic bottles. Hannah: It sounds good, but I read that once the bottles have been turned into polyester, the clothes usually can't be recycled again, and they shed tiny plastic fibres when you wash them. So it's not nearly as green as the advertising suggests. Leo: Mm. Then there's digital fashion, clothes that only exist online, for people to wear in photos on social media. Hannah: I can't see that catching on widely. A few gamers and influencers might buy them, but most people won't be interested. Leo: The report also talked about brands giving customers information about where their clothes are made, like which factory. Hannah: Some brands do, but most still keep it very vague. They really need to tell people more, because customers want to know whether workers are being treated fairly. Leo: And the last one was the huge growth in ultra-cheap clothing sold online. Hannah: That worries me. Tests on some of those items have found high levels of harmful chemicals, even in children's clothes. They could actually make people ill. Leo: That's a good point to finish on. I think I'll use some of this in the introduction to my dissertation. Shall we meet again next week and compare notes? Hannah: Sounds good. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear an archaeology student giving a presentation about an ancient village in Scotland called Skara Brae. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation today, I'm going to talk about Skara Brae, a Neolithic village on the main island of Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland. It's one of the best-preserved prehistoric villages in Europe, and I was lucky enough to visit it last summer. Today, it forms part of a World Heritage Site that also includes several other Neolithic monuments nearby, such as two great stone circles and a huge chambered tomb. Student: For thousands of years, the village lay hidden under sand dunes beside a bay on the west coast of the island. Then, in the winter of eighteen fifty, a great storm struck Orkney. The wind and waves stripped the grass and sand from a large mound, revealing the stone walls of several ancient houses. The local landowner, William Watt, became interested and began excavating the site, and over the next few years he uncovered four of the houses. Student: However, work then stopped for many years, and it was only after another storm damaged some of the houses in nineteen twenty-four that a proper investigation began. A sea wall was built to protect the site from the waves, and a team led by the archaeologist Gordon Childe excavated the village in the late nineteen twenties. Later, radiocarbon dating showed that people had lived there for around six hundred years, from roughly three thousand one hundred BCE, which means the village is older than the Great Pyramid of Egypt. Student: The village consisted of eight houses, linked by low, covered passages. Walking through them, you have to bend down, and it's easy to imagine how well they protected people from the wind. Each house was a single square room with a hearth in the centre. The hearth was used for both heating and cooking, and the smoke probably escaped through a hole in the roof, which may have been covered with turf or animal skins. What makes Skara Brae really special, though, is the furniture. Because there were very few trees on Orkney, almost everything was made of stone. There are stone beds on either side of the hearth, which may have been filled with heather or straw, stone boxes set into the floor for storage, and a stone dresser facing the door, which may have been used to display the family's most precious objects. Student: People often assume the houses would have been cold and damp, but they were actually well insulated. The villagers packed a thick layer of their household rubbish, which archaeologists call midden, around the outside walls, and this helped to keep the heat in. In fact, the midden was so solid that the houses were partly sunk into it, which also gave them extra protection from the strong winds that sweep across the islands for much of the year. Student: The inhabitants were farmers who kept cattle and sheep and grew barley, and they also ate fish and shellfish. Metal wasn't available to them, as this was long before the Bronze Age, so they made tools and jewellery out of bone, including needles, beads and pins. There's even evidence of a drainage system running beneath the houses, and some archaeologists think that small cells in the walls may have been used as toilets, which would make them among the earliest known in Britain. Student: So why was the village abandoned, around two thousand five hundred BCE? There's a popular story that the villagers left in a great hurry, because a string of beads was found scattered in one of the passages, as if a necklace had broken as someone rushed out. But most archaeologists now believe that people left gradually, over a long period. One likely reason is that the climate became colder and wetter, which would have made farming more difficult. Another is that sand gradually blew in from the dunes and began to cover the fields and even the houses themselves. Whatever the reason, the same sand that may have driven the villagers away went on to preserve their homes for nearly five thousand years. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

But the sponsored walk beat everything, with nearly twelve hundred pounds. Thank you to everyone who took part. Chair: Next month, we'll be welcoming the Bergen choir here, and many of you have kindly offered to host singers. Their coach arrives at the community centre at six on Friday, so there's no need to go to the airport. On Saturday morning, there's a rehearsal at ten, but please don't feel you have to arrive early. After the rehearsal, we're taking everyone on a walking tour of the old town. The cafe in the market square is providing lunch, so there's no need to make sandwiches. The forecast isn't good, though, so please make sure your guests have waterproof clothing with them. Chair: On Sunday afternoon, we'll give our joint concert. Unfortunately, the children's choir from Saint Mark's School can't join us after all, as several of the children will be away. But I'm pleased to say that the local radio station will be recording the concert, and they'll broadcast part of it the following week. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Chair: The concert will be in Bramley Hall, in Bramley Park, and I've given you all a map, because some of our guests will want to explore the park before the concert starts. Chair: As you come in through the main gate, you'll see a small building immediately on your left, right beside the gate. That's the ticket office, and that's where the Bergen singers should collect their passes. Chair: Some of our guests use wheelchairs, and there are steps at the front of the hall, so they'll need the accessible entrance. That's at the back of the hall, on the side furthest from the main gate. Just follow the path round. Chair: If any of your guests have children with them, there's a good playground. Walk along the cross path to the right, all the way to the end, then turn left and go north, with the lake on your left. At the top, the path bends to the left, and the playground is just there, beyond the northern end of the lake. Chair: We're planning a picnic before the concert, weather permitting. We'll meet on the lawn between the hall and the lake, on the east side of the hall. Chair: And for anyone who fancies a walk, there's an old tower in the park with wonderful views. Take the cross path to the left, all the way to the end, and then turn right. That path goes north along the edge of the woods, and the tower is at the very end, in the corner of the park. Chair: Right, if there are no questions, let's move on to the music for next season. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two fashion design students, Hannah and Leo, discussing their final-year projects. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Hannah: Hi, Leo. I haven't seen you in the studio for ages. Leo: No, I've been working at home mostly. The final project has taken over my life. Hannah: You're making bags out of old jeans, aren't you? Leo: That's right. I collect jeans that people have thrown out, cut them up and turn them into bags. The actual sewing was fairly straightforward. I've been using the embroidery machine to decorate them, but I learned how to use that in the first year, so that wasn't new. Hannah: So what's been the best part? Leo: Honestly, the thing I'm proudest of is taking something that was going to end up in landfill and turning it into something people actually want to use. That's really satisfying. And I've loved trying out different ways of decorating the bags, like painting, patchwork and embroidery. Every bag's different. I've made about thirty so far, and I'm hoping to have fifty for the final exhibition. Hannah: Have you entered it for the college prize? Leo: Yes, but they won't announce the winners until June, so I'm not getting my hopes up. And I've been working completely on my own, which has been a bit lonely, to be honest. Hannah: Well, I think the bags sound great. My project's quite different. I've been looking at fabrics that change colour depending on temperature. Leo: Oh, using special dyes? Hannah: Yes. They've been around for decades, but people mainly thought of them as a novelty, like T-shirts that changed colour when you touched them. Some designers have used them in catwalk shows too, but that's really just for effect. Leo: I remember those T-shirts. So what could they be used for now? Hannah: Well, one idea is sportswear, so that coaches could see which muscles are working hardest. Leo: I'm not convinced by that. Athletes already have heart monitors and all sorts of sensors that give much more accurate information. Hannah: Maybe you're right. But I think they'd be really useful in clothes for babies. If a baby was getting a fever, the fabric would change colour, and parents would notice straight away. Leo: Yes, that's a great idea. Parents would definitely buy that. And what about hospitals? Bandages that change colour to show when a wound is getting infected? Hannah: That's already being researched, actually. And I agree, I think that's where the real future is. Leo: It's certainly more useful than handbags that change colour in the sun. Hannah: Ha, yes. Someone tried that a few years ago, and nobody bought them. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Leo: I've been reading a report on trends in the fashion industry for my dissertation. My tutor wants us to connect our own projects to what is happening in the wider industry, so it has been really useful. Hannah: Oh, that sounds interesting. What did it say? Leo: Well, one trend is the growth in apps for buying and selling second-hand clothes. Hannah: That's hardly new, is it? My sister and her friends have been using those apps for years. Leo: True. Then there's the question of what brands do with clothes they can't sell. Some of them just burn them or shred them. Hannah: That's terrible. France has banned it, hasn't it? I think our government should bring in a law like that, too. Leo: I agree. Another trend is clothing made from recycled plastic bottles. Hannah: It sounds good, but I read that once the bottles have been turned into polyester, the clothes usually can't be recycled again, and they shed tiny plastic fibres when you wash them. So it's not nearly as green as the advertising suggests. Leo: Mm. Then there's digital fashion, clothes that only exist online, for people to wear in photos on social media. Hannah: I can't see that catching on widely. A few gamers and influencers might buy them, but most people won't be interested. Leo: The report also talked about brands giving customers information about where their clothes are made, like which factory. Hannah: Some brands do, but most still keep it very vague. They really need to tell people more, because customers want to know whether workers are being treated fairly. Leo: And the last one was the huge growth in ultra-cheap clothing sold online. Hannah: That worries me. Tests on some of those items have found high levels of harmful chemicals, even in children's clothes. They could actually make people ill. Leo: That's a good point to finish on. I think I'll use some of this in the introduction to my dissertation. Shall we meet again next week and compare notes? Hannah: Sounds good. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear an archaeology student giving a presentation about an ancient village in Scotland called Skara Brae. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation today, I'm going to talk about Skara Brae, a Neolithic village on the main island of Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland. It's one of the best-preserved prehistoric villages in Europe, and I was lucky enough to visit it last summer. Today, it forms part of a World Heritage Site that also includes several other Neolithic monuments nearby, such as two great stone circles and a huge chambered tomb. Student: For thousands of years, the village lay hidden under sand dunes beside a bay on the west coast of the island. Then, in the winter of eighteen fifty, a great storm struck Orkney. The wind and waves stripped the grass and sand from a large mound, revealing the stone walls of several ancient houses. The local landowner, William Watt, became interested and began excavating the site, and over the next few years he uncovered four of the houses. Student: However, work then stopped for many years, and it was only after another storm damaged some of the houses in nineteen twenty-four that a proper investigation began. A sea wall was built to protect the site from the waves, and a team led by the archaeologist Gordon Childe excavated the village in the late nineteen twenties. Later, radiocarbon dating showed that people had lived there for around six hundred years, from roughly three thousand one hundred BCE, which means the village is older than the Great Pyramid of Egypt. Student: The village consisted of eight houses, linked by low, covered passages. Walking through them, you have to bend down, and it's easy to imagine how well they protected people from the wind. Each house was a single square room with a hearth in the centre. The hearth was used for both heating and cooking, and the smoke probably escaped through a hole in the roof, which may have been covered with turf or animal skins. What makes Skara Brae really special, though, is the furniture. Because there were very few trees on Orkney, almost everything was made of stone. There are stone beds on either side of the hearth, which may have been filled with heather or straw, stone boxes set into the floor for storage, and a stone dresser facing the door, which may have been used to display the family's most precious objects. Student: People often assume the houses would have been cold and damp, but they were actually well insulated. The villagers packed a thick layer of their household rubbish, which archaeologists call midden, around the outside walls, and this helped to keep the heat in. In fact, the midden was so solid that the houses were partly sunk into it, which also gave them extra protection from the strong winds that sweep across the islands for much of the year. Student: The inhabitants were farmers who kept cattle and sheep and grew barley, and they also ate fish and shellfish. Metal wasn't available to them, as this was long before the Bronze Age, so they made tools and jewellery out of bone, including needles, beads and pins. There's even evidence of a drainage system running beneath the houses, and some archaeologists think that small cells in the walls may have been used as toilets, which would make them among the earliest known in Britain. Student: So why was the village abandoned, around two thousand five hundred BCE? There's a popular story that the villagers left in a great hurry, because a string of beads was found scattered in one of the passages, as if a necklace had broken as someone rushed out. But most archaeologists now believe that people left gradually, over a long period. One likely reason is that the climate became colder and wetter, which would have made farming more difficult. Another is that sand gradually blew in from the dunes and began to cover the fields and even the houses themselves. Whatever the reason, the same sand that may have driven the villagers away went on to preserve their homes for nearly five thousand years. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
